summary:
Lampung province stands under Indonesia's national framework. The province's own record of official conduct toward transgender people includes a November 2018 operation in which the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at its Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident.

OutRight International's study of discriminatory regional regulations names Lampung among eight Indonesian provinces where such rules operate, examined at both province and district level. A trans visitor in Lampung is therefore subject to two layers of provincial regulation in addition to the national framework.
tangentialFactors:
The Lampung raid does not stand alone. The same human-rights review documents trans women murdered in 2017 in Bone, Semarang and South Sulawesi, and records anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying tied to election cycles in Indonesia from 2016 onward, indicating that regional regulation of gender and sexuality has been an active political project across multiple provinces rather than a Lampung-only phenomenon.

Public hostility provides the backdrop: an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians conducted in November 2016 found that 16.6% of respondents said they hated LGBT people. The figure is a national sample with no Lampung breakdown, and it measures stated attitude rather than incidence of violence.
localsOnly:
Satpol PP functions as Lampung's regional morals-and-order force, and the November 2018 detention and hosing of three trans women was carried out by its officers at provincial facilities, with an officer filming the act. Residents of the province deal with this force directly, and the incident shows provincial officials recording their own conduct rather than acting to conceal it.

OutRight International examined Lampung's discriminatory regional regulations at both province and district level, so residents are exposed to two tiers of local rule-making on gender and sexuality, not one.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific provisions of the Lampung regulations identified by OutRight International are unresolved in the sources reviewed: the study names the province among eight, but the inventory does not reproduce the text of the rules or state what conduct they prohibit.

Whether the November 2018 raid on the three trans women produced any prosecution, disciplinary action or remedy is not sourced. No outcome, charge or inquiry is recorded.

No Lampung-specific data was identified on the frequency of Satpol PP operations against trans people after 2018, on hate-crime designation of anti-trans offences in the province, or on any screening or document treatment specific to Lampung's own entry points.
